name: 6th Sunday of Easter
description: Prayer Sunday. Jesus' High Priestly Prayer.
biblicalBasis: Jesus prays his great prayer for the disciples and all who will come to believe (John 17): "Holy Father, keep them in your name... that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you." The promise: "Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete" (John 16:24). "Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive."
significance: The High Priestly Prayer reveals Jesus' deepest desire: unity among believers, rooted in the unity between the Father and the Son. Prayer is not about persuading God, but entering into the fellowship between Father and Son through the Spirit. Joy does not depend on circumstances but on our relationship with God.
liturgicalContext: White color. The last Sunday before Ascension in some traditions. Rogation Days (days of prayer) fall during this week in the Western Church—prayers for the year's harvest and God's blessing.
history: Rogation Days (the three days before Ascension) were introduced by Bishop Mamertus in Vienne around 470, originally as a prayer and penitential procession in response to natural disasters. They later became a fixed part of the church calendar with a focus on praying for daily bread.
otConnections: Solomon's temple dedication prayer (1 Kings 8:22-53)—a prayer for the entire people in God's presence. Abraham's intercession for Sodom (Genesis 18:22-33). Moses' intercession for the people after the golden calf incident (Exodus 32:11-14). Daniel's prayer for the restoration of Jerusalem (Daniel 9:1-19).

references.reason: Verses 19-20 promise that the Father's Spirit will speak through the disciples. This is a central theme during Easter, especially in the period leading up to Pentecost (6th Sunday), where the Spirit as witness and speaker is the main focus. The text emphasizes that believers are not alone in their testimony.
